articles.title: Initiatives of Uzbekistan aimed at Economic Results for the Countries of Central Asia and Azerbaijan - DKNews.kz
articles.summary: Initiatives of Uzbekistan aimed at Economic Results for the Countries of Central Asia and Azerbaijan  DKNews.kz
articles.full_text:
On October 8–9, President Shavkat Mirziyoyev attended the 8th Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, as well as a meeting of the CIS Council of Heads of State.
The consultative meetings stem from an initiative put forward by the President of Uzbekistan in 2017. The first meeting took place in Astana in March 2018. This framework allows countries to work together on transit, infrastructure use, border procedures and industrial cooperation where the involvement of several countries is required.
At the seventh meeting, held in Tashkent on November 16, 2025, participants agreed to Azerbaijan’s full participation. This creates opportunities to coordinate industrial development in Central Asia with transport infrastructure in the South Caucasus and routes to markets in Türkiye and Europe.
For businesses, transport arrangements need to be coordinated along the entire route. Faster customs clearance in one country will have limited benefits if cargo is held up at the next border or port. Joint ventures also need coordinated arrangements for raw material supplies, certification and financing. Expanding the group of participants therefore makes multilateral coordination more useful in practice.
Expanding Trade and the Regional Market
According to the Center for Economic Research and Reforms (CERR), Uzbekistan’s trade with Central Asian countries grew 3.1-fold between 2017 and 2025, reaching $8.3 billion. In 2025, trade with Kazakhstan totaled $5 billion, with Kyrgyzstan and Turkmenistan $1.2 billion each, and with Tajikistan $912.3 million.
In January–August 2026, trade with the four neighboring countries reached $6.14 billion, up 26.2% from the same period a year earlier. Uzbekistan’s exports rose 37.5% to $2.36 billion, while imports increased 20.1% to $3.78 billion. Trade grew with every partner: Kazakhstan by 23.4%, Kyrgyzstan by 51.2%, Tajikistan by 45.7% and Turkmenistan by 5.7%.
Trade with Azerbaijan grew 9.5-fold between 2017 and 2025, reaching $307.3 million. In 2025, Uzbekistan’s exports totaled $227.3 million and imports $80 million. Established trade in machinery, textiles, food and metals provides a basis for greater specialization among businesses and joint efforts to promote their products. Long-term contracts, well-developed distribution networks and equipment servicing in the partner country can support more sustained growth.
Investment and Production Links
Between 2017 and 2025, Uzbekistan attracted $2.5 billion in foreign direct investment and loans from Central Asian countries, including $1.3 billion in 2025. The corresponding figures for Azerbaijan were $318.6 million and $173.7 million. As of August 2026, Uzbekistan had 2,538 operating companies with investment from Central Asian countries and 503 with Azerbaijani investment.
The Azerbaijan–Uzbekistan Investment Company supports joint projects and has charter capital of $500 million. Joint investment institutions also operate in Central Asia, including Uzbek–Kyrgyz and Uzbek–Tajik institutions. They enable partners to finance projects together and share risks.
Practical Steps Since the Tashkent Meeting
On November 17, 2025, Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan launched the Shavat–Dashoguz border trade zone. It houses trading and warehousing facilities, customs, quarantine and other inspection services. Government services are to be provided through a single-window system.
On March 26, 2026, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan launched ten joint projects in furniture, leather and textile production, household appliances and other industries. At the same time, facilities were launched to produce dairy products in Andijan Region, and fruit juices and metal briquettes in Surkhandarya Region.
During Uzbek–Kyrgyz talks on July 30, 2026, the two sides agreed to establish an Interstate Council. A package of trade contracts and investment agreements was put together at the preceding business forum. They also reached agreements on developing border, trade and logistics infrastructure along the China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan railway and digitizing permit procedures.
On July 31, 2026, the leaders of Central Asia and Azerbaijan held an informal meeting at Issyk-Kul. The President of Uzbekistan called for further work on industrial and technological production chains, shared digital services and investment platforms.
On August 23, 2026, Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan signed a program to increase trade to $1 billion by 2030, along with an action plan for investment and trade. The third meeting of the Supreme Interstate Council also launched joint projects in finance, building materials, oil and gas, mining, agriculture and other sectors.
Industrial Cooperation and Access to New Markets
CERR estimates that replacing some imports from third countries with supplies from within the region could increase intraregional trade by approximately $11.4 billion. Realizing this potential will depend on whether regional suppliers can compete. This requires matching imported products with what regional producers can offer and identifying barriers to concluding contracts.
Developing the Middle Corridor through the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus could expand Uzbekistan’s opportunities to supply markets to the west. The route’s competitiveness depends on the total cost of delivery, regular departures and transit times along each section. This requires coordination among railways, ports, carriers and customs services.
Joint preparations for the Kambarata-1 hydropower plant and work on Uzbek–Tajik hydropower projects require agreement on financing, water use arrangements and electricity supply terms. Investment decisions need to reflect growing industrial demand and businesses’ need for reliable energy supplies.
An interagency working group has also been established to prepare joint green energy projects involving Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan.
Priorities for the Upcoming Meeting
The upcoming meeting in Avaza offers an opportunity to advance joint projects by addressing trade barriers, coordinating transport arrangements and securing financing. Moving beyond separate bilateral projects to align business conditions across the expanded group of participating countries could help advance these efforts.
Projects backed by proven demand, competitive production and reliable logistics can deliver the most tangible economic benefits. The regional mechanisms proposed by Uzbekistan could support these projects by removing trade barriers, coordinating infrastructure development and improving investment conditions. Under these conditions, growth in trade within the region would be accompanied by more value added within the region and a stronger position for its producers in international markets.
Edvard Romanov
Center for Economic Research and Reforms

articles.title: Ukraine War, Day 1,699: Trump — “Russia Has Been Fine. They Haven’t Been Doing Much” - EA WorldView
articles.summary: Ukraine War, Day 1,699: Trump — “Russia Has Been Fine. They Haven’t Been Doing Much”  EA WorldView
articles.full_text:
Donald Trump at a rally in Kansas, October 19, 2026 (Sky)
UPDATE 1358 GMT:
Officials have confirmed that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has not approved the transfer of Patriot interceptor missiles by other countries to Ukraine.
One US official and “three additional people familiar with the situation” confirmed the hold-up. American permission is required for any movement of the US-made Patriots.
The sources said Hegseth has not formally rejected the transfers but also has not completed the required steps to approve them.
UPDATE 0834 GMT:
At least one civilian was murdered and six injured by a Russian drone strike on early-morning commuter traffic in the Holosiivskyi district of Kyiv.
The drone crashed near a gas station. Images showed multiple cars ablaze near the Kyiv-Odesa highway.
Earlier in the morning, two women and a man were killed and at least six people injured by a Russian attack on a production and warehouse building in the city of Obukhiv, just south of Kyiv.
Russia attacked Ukraine overnight with 165 drones, 105 of them jet-powered. Air defenses downed or suppressed 115 of the UAVs, 73 of them jet-powered.
UPDATE 0828 GMT:
Ukraine’s drones have set afire an oil pumping station near the city of Michurinsk in Russia’s Tambov region overnight.
Tambov Governor Yevgeny Pervyshov acknowledged the fire “on the territory of one of the enterprises” without giving details.
Video showed fire and dark smoke, with residents identifying a diesel fuel tank. Independent Russian outlet ASTRA said the fire likely started at the Nikolskoye-1 linear production and dispatch station.
UPDATE 0821 GMT:
Ahead of his meeting in Oslo with Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has spoken with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio:
Zelensky praised “a substantive conversation focused on the issues that matter”. He expressed gratitude for Rubio’s “readiness to help and his clear position”, including with ballistic missile interceptors, early-warning intelligence, and the restoration of Starlink and Starshield.
UPDATE 0814 GMT:
In an interview with Italy’s Corriere della Sera, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has sent a message to the US:
We have always had important, strong strategic relations with the United States of America. Our bilateral relationship began developing particularly actively during the full-scale war. I am grateful for all the support.
But we have always built our relationship on honesty, fairness, and, most importantly, transparency. Because when you lie while your people are at war, it is very painful. That is why I have always wanted to hide nothing and never lie to the President of the United States. In any case, we have more in common than America does with Russia. Most people in Ukraine and the United States of America understand this. We would like to continue having the same open, honest, and pragmatic relations with America that we have today.
The position is very simple. We support a mutual energy ceasefire. If we are talking about the idea that we should not strike back at Russian energy facilities after they strike our gas, electricity, oil – everything. The Russians are striking. America cannot stop them. Let’s believe that America really wants to, but cannot. Then, as a partner, I am willing to meet President Trump halfway: if they strike us and we cannot strike back – that is neither honest nor fair – but if this is what you need, if you cannot rein Putin in, then give us interceptor missiles so I can protect our energy infrastructure. You couldn’t stop Putin – but you helped Ukraine.
From an interview with Corriere della Sera. (2/3)
— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 20, 2026
Zelensky also warned about Russian propaganda in Europe:
People should not be pierced through and brainwashed by waves of narratives from the Russian Federation. Because it is up to France, Ukraine, Italy, and Spain to decide how to live and whom to elect. Russia cannot influence Italy’s choices and freedom. Italy is a free country, just like Ukraine.
UPDATE 0803 GMT:
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky updated Pope Leo XIV in a phone call on Monday.
On Friday, the Pope spoke with Vladimir Putin to propose a ceasefire in Oleshky, the Russian-occupied frontline town in the Kherson region in southern Ukraine. Around 2,000 residents are trapped without sufficient supplies of food or medicine, reportedly as Russian troops confiscate aid dropped by the Ukrainian military.
Zelensky and the Pope discussed the humanitarian emergency unfolding in Oleshky, including the Vatican’s diplomatic efforts with Russia.
“We are working to help our people there and are preparing solutions,” Zelensky said. “His Holiness informed me about his contacts with the Russian side regarding this issue.”
UPDATE 0751 GMT:
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky met virtually with US legislators on Monday to evaluate Donald Trump’s tilt towards Russia’s invasion.
The meeting, including Democrats and Republicans from the Senate and the House of Representatives, was organized by Democrat Sen. Richard Blumenthal and Republican Sen. Thom Tillis.
Zelensky spoke about delayed deliveries of US-made Patriot interceptors, ongoing restrictions to Starshield access for Ukrainian frontline forces, and the abrupt end to warnings about Russian missile launches.
He cited “the most difficult situation since the very beginning of this war”.
Zelensky noted progress by Ukraine’s forces on the frontlines in the east of the country. However, the Trump-assisted disasters “stand in sharp contrast to what we are achieving on the battlefield”.
[You] need to understand how serious this is….Russia’s attacks have become even more vicious and dirty.
There is hardly an hour when Russia isn’t attacking somewhere or hitting something. And this happens every single day.
ORIGINAL ENTRY: Swinging to support of Moscow’s 56-month full-scale invasion, Donald Trump says, “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much.”
Trump spoke to reporters on Monday, just after a Russian daytime drone strike on a park in Kharkiv that killed six people, including three children, and injured 15, including seven juveniles. Overnight, Russia attacked Kyiv with more than 12 ballistic missiles and targeted almost 30 critical energy facilities across Ukraine.
Since October 9, with the Kremlin offering deal worth tens of billions of dollars profiting associates of his family and friends, Trump has undermined US sanctions and agreed to purchase of Russian diesel oil. Early-warning intelligence has been cut at times, amid Russia’s missile and drone strikes threatening US personnel as well as Ukraine’s civilians. The military version of Starlink, Starshield, has been restricted.
Trump said he is open to a trilateral meeting, proposed by the Kremlin, with Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. He said the main purpose of the meeting would be discussion of nuclear disarmament.
Trump said of Xi, “He’s been very fair with Ukraine. He hasn’t been much involved, and same with Russia.”
He then made a garbled assertion, “They haven’t been nearly what they could have been, and I appreciate that.” It was unclear if he was referring to China or Russia.
Trump: "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much." https://t.co/1UpyCwoF1h
— Aaron Rupar (@atrupar) October 19, 2026
Trump promoted his recent support of the Kremlin, citing negotiations for the release of a high-profile hostage. He insisted, in defiance of US intelligence, that Russia was “very well-behaved on Iran” and Putin was “laying off” amid the US war.
US officials have spoken of Russia’s shipment of weapons to Iran, aid in Tehran’s missile development, and provision of intelligence to help Iran attack US bases and troops in the Middle East. Joint Chiefs of Staff chair Gen. Dan Caine has confirmed the support.
But Trump declared, “Russia’s done nothing there that we can see, and I think that’s a very positive….Russia could have done a lot more to help Iran. Russia’s done very little for Iran.”
He continued his verbal assault on Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky, “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. They’ve given nothing to us.”
Witkoff To Meet Zelensky and Europe Officials
Trump’s envoy, real estate developer Steve Witkoff, will meet Zelensky and European officials in Norway’s capital Oslo on Tuesday.
Witkoff will then convene with Putin in the Kremlin.
During his last meeting with Ukrainian and European officials on October 9, Witkoff announced Trump’s diesel deal. He threatened a cutoff of US intelligence sharing if Ukraine did not halt attacks on Russian refineries.
Ukraine suspended the strikes for 72 hours but then, with Trump backing Moscow, resumed attacks including on Russia’s third-largest refinery in St. Petersburg.
The talks in Oslo today will also include Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre; representatives of the UK, France, Germany, and Poland; and officials from the European Union and NATO.
Trump’s other envoy, son-in-law Jared Kushner, has the flu and will participate virtually.
Continuing its manipulation of Trump and his envoys, the Kremlin is dangling the possibility of the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired American teacher who has been detained in Russia since 2022.
Hubbard was reportedly been serving with a Ukrainian territorial defense unit in the Kharkiv region in northeast Ukraine when he was seized by Russian forces.

Trump should be impeached

articles.title: Mirziyoyev awards Rubio and Gor state honors for strengthening U.S.-Uzbekistan ties - Daryo
articles.summary: Mirziyoyev awards Rubio and Gor state honors for strengthening U.S.-Uzbekistan ties  Daryo
articles.full_text:
Uzbekistan’s President Shavkat Mirziyoyev has awarded U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio the Order “Buyuk xizmatlari uchun” (Order "For Great Services") and U.S. Presidential Special Representative for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor the Order “Do‘stlik” (Order of Friendship), recognizing their contributions to strengthening strategic ties between Uzbekistan and the United States, the presidential press service reported.
Rubio received the Order For Great Services for his contribution to developing the strategic partnership between the two countries and expanding political, diplomatic, trade, economic, cultural, and humanitarian cooperation.
His support for efforts to promote peace, stability, and sustainable development in Central Asia was also recognized, alongside his role in advancing Uzbekistan’s international initiatives and strengthening trust and friendship between the two peoples.
Gor was awarded the Order of Friendship for his efforts to strengthen friendly relations and expand the strategic partnership between Uzbekistan and the United States.
His contributions included intensifying political dialogue, implementing bilateral agreements, attracting U.S. investors, and promoting joint projects. His role in developing cooperation through the U.S.-Uzbekistan Business and Investment Council was also highlighted.

articles.title: EU-Backed Infrastructure Strengthens Azerbaijan–Central Asia Connectivity - The Jamestown Foundation
articles.summary: EU-Backed Infrastructure Strengthens Azerbaijan–Central Asia Connectivity  The Jamestown Foundation
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary:
- At an EU–Uzbekistan conference in Tashkent on September 30, officials signaled that the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor is shifting from political commitments to implementation, backed by growing European bank financing in Uzbekistan.
- In Kazakhstan, German logistics firm Rhenus Group and local partners agreed to advance a planned container terminal at Aktau, and Rhenus plans 14 terminals along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, where cargo volumes rose 58 percent year on year.
- The European Union proposed a connectivity partnership with Azerbaijan and announced up to 200 million euros ($225 million) in South Caucasus grants, with possible projects including the Nakhchivan railway and Port of Baku.
On September 30, the European Union and Uzbekistan convened the Second National Conference on the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor in Tashkent, bringing together government officials, international financial institutions, development partners, and the private sector. The European Union uses this name for its connectivity agenda along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), also known as the Middle Corridor. The meeting underscored the corridor’s shift from political commitments toward implementation, with a focus on converting shared priorities into investable projects. European Commission Director for Asia and the Pacific Pēteris Ustubs noted the corridor is “moving from ambition to implementation,” with growing emphasis on “concrete projects” and “real investment on the ground” (European External Action Service, September 30).
Discussions covered railway and road infrastructure, logistics centers, border-crossing procedures, digital transport documents, and greater private-sector participation. The conference was held within the EU-funded Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor Coordination Platform, which operates under Global Gateway, the European Union’s global infrastructure investment strategy. The platform brings together the five Central Asian states, the European Union, international financial institutions, and other partners (European External Action Service, September 30).
The conference took place amid growing European financial support for Uzbekistan’s transport sector. In June, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBDR) approved a loan of up to 38.4 million euros ($43.1 million) for the digital transformation of Uzbekistan Railways. The project will introduce modern traffic-management systems, including dispatching, scheduling, and operational control, while strengthening cybersecurity. Uzbekistan Railways operates a 6,950-kilometer (4,318-mile) network and handles up to 40 percent of the country’s freight, making its modernization relevant to cargo flows toward the Caspian (EBDR, June 17).
European financial engagement with Uzbekistan could expand further. In June, the European Investment Bank opened its Central Asian regional representation in Tashkent and announced that its regional project pipeline was approaching 3 billion euros ($3.37 billion). Potential operations under consideration in Uzbekistan total around 1 billion euros ($1.12 billion) and include transport, energy, climate, digital connectivity, and critical raw materials, with the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor among the priorities (European External Action Service; European Investment Bank, June 18)
Uzbekistan is also exploring additional links to Azerbaijan across the Caspian. During the September 30 conference, Uztemiryolkonteyner, the state-controlled container freight subsidiary of Uzbekistan Railways, proposed regular feeder services between Turkmenbashi, Turkmenistan, and Baku, Azerbaijan, to expand multimodal transport between Uzbekistan and Europe. “The organization of regular feeder services between Turkmenbashi and Baku will create additional opportunities to accelerate cargo delivery, expand multimodal transportation and strengthen Uzbekistan’s connectivity with European markets,” the company said at the conference (Trend News Agency, September 30).
Kazakhstan is advancing larger-scale infrastructure projects along the Caspian section of TITR. On September 30, German logistics company Rhenus Group, Kazakhstan’s national railway company Kazakhstan Temir Zholy, and the Port of Aktau agreed to move forward with a new trimodal container terminal in Aktau. The planned facility would cover at least 30 hectares (74 acres), integrate rail, road, and maritime transport, and provide at least 150,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU) of additional annual handling capacity. Rhenus links the project to TITR and the European Union’s Global Gateway initiative. Rhenus Group Chief Executive Officer Tobias Bartz said the challenge is “to bring individual infrastructure projects together step by step into an efficient network,” with Kazakhstan playing a key role in connecting the People’s Republic of China, Central Asia, the Caspian region, and Europe (Rhenus Logistics, September 30).
Rhenus’ plans extend beyond Aktau. Bartz said the company intends to develop 14 terminals along sections of TITR across Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, and Türkiye. “After that, they will be connected to our company’s networks in Europe. Rhenus has 23 container terminals and 70 port facilities there. This project will connect the logistics networks of Central Asia and Europe into a single network,” he said (Azernews, October 1).
Traffic volumes are also rising. About 44,000 TEU were transported via TITR in the first eight months of 2026, up 58 percent year on year, Kazakhstan Temir Zholy Deputy Chairman Yerlan Koyshibayev said at the Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in Baku on September 25. He highlighted the corridor’s role in strengthening transport and logistics links between “Central Asia, the Caucasus, and European markets” (Trend News Agency, September 26).
The European Union is deepening its connectivity engagement with Azerbaijan. During her May visit to Baku, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said there was “clear scope to deepen our cooperation, particularly on trade, transport and digital,” adding that stronger connectivity between “the EU, the South Caucasus, and Central Asia” was a shared strategic interest (European External Action Service, May 5).
That approach became more concrete in July. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed an EU–Azerbaijan Connectivity Partnership and a High-Level Connectivity Dialogue covering transport, energy, and digital connectivity. Under Global Gateway, she announced up to 200 million euros ($225 million) in grants for South Caucasus connectivity projects, with the potential to mobilize up to 2 billion euros ($2.25 billion) in public and private investment. Possible projects include the railway connection through Nakhchivan and the “development of the Port of Baku” (European Commission, July 1).
The Nakhchivan railway had already entered the preparatory stage in January, when the European Union, Azerbaijan, and the EBRD agreed to launch a feasibility study. The European Union describes the railway as part of the broader Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor linking Europe and Central Asia (European Commission, January 29). Von der Leyen also announced plans for a Regional Connectivity Investment Conference in Baku, bringing together Europe, the South Caucasus, and Central Asia.
The TITR is moving from political ambition toward a more integrated transport system. European-backed modernization in Uzbekistan, German-led logistics investment in Kazakhstan, and the European Union’s expanding connectivity agenda with Azerbaijan are strengthening the Central Asia–Caspian–South Caucasus link. The next stage will be to deepen coordination and connect these projects into an increasingly seamless corridor between Central Asia and Europe.

articles.title: Uzbekistan and the United States: Why New Investment Agreements Could Reshape Central Asia’s Economic Landscape - UzDaily.uz
articles.summary: Uzbekistan and the United States: Why New Investment Agreements Could Reshape Central Asia’s Economic Landscape  UzDaily.uz
articles.full_text:
Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — The second meeting of the US–Uzbekistan Business and Investment Council took place in Samarkand on 19 October 2026. Its most visible outcome was a package of 54 agreements and prospective initiatives worth approximately US$12 billion. Yet the significance of the meeting lies less in the headline figure than in the industries targeted and the possibility that American capital could alter Uzbekistan’s position in regional production networks.
President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, presidential special envoy Sergio Gor and representatives of American companies attended the meeting. The visit coincided with a C5+1 ministerial gathering, giving a bilateral economic agenda a wider regional dimension. Tashkent is seeking technology and new financing channels; Washington is looking to expand its commercial presence in a region already connected to Chinese, Russian, European and Gulf investors.
Why Is Washington Expanding Its Economic Engagement Now?
Central Asia is becoming more relevant to global industry for reasons extending beyond conventional energy resources. It combines mineral deposits, important Eurasian transport routes and growing domestic markets. For the United States, these advantages are increasingly significant as companies and policymakers seek to diversify supplies of materials used in electronics, energy systems and advanced manufacturing.
In Samarkand, Marco Rubio highlighted the risks of excessive concentration in critical-mineral supply chains. The American rationale is pragmatic: a broader group of partners can reduce dependence on a narrow set of suppliers. Uzbekistan, meanwhile, wants to move beyond extracting and exporting raw materials towards processing and higher-value manufacturing.
The distinction matters. Additional extraction may increase export revenues without necessarily creating an advanced industrial base. Processing facilities, technology transfer, engineering education and local suppliers could generate a more durable economic return. The quality of the eventual projects will therefore matter more than their announced value.
Twelve Billion Dollars: Investment or Intentions?
The $12 billion figure covers agreements and prospective initiatives assembled for the council meeting. According to Mirziyoyev, 45 Uzbek ministries and agencies participated in the preparatory work, and American companies were paired with potential partners in government, regional administrations and business. This indicates substantial coordination, but it does not mean that $12 billion in foreign direct investment has already entered the economy.
Between a signed document and an operating plant lie feasibility studies, financing decisions, permits, infrastructure construction and commissioning. Some initiatives may change in scope or timing; others may never reach implementation. The proper measures of success will be capital actually deployed, employment generated and products manufactured, rather than the initial total of announced commitments.
Tashkent is also proposing a plug-and-play model under which investors receive prepared sites with infrastructure and documentation in place. This could shorten project lead times. Its effectiveness, however, will depend on predictable regulation, reliable electricity, credible dispute resolution and the ability to repatriate returns. Administrative readiness cannot substitute for a sound investment climate.
Critical Minerals: Raw Exports or Industrial Transformation?
A central priority is to develop a chain running from mineral extraction to advanced products. For Uzbekistan, this creates an opportunity to strengthen not only mining but also domestic processing. Cooperation with American research and industrial institutions could support modern exploration techniques, improve efficiency and expand the pool of trained engineers.
Nevertheless, processing requires dependable and competitively priced electricity, water, transport access and skilled labour. If these conditions are missing, investors may prefer to export concentrates for processing elsewhere. This is where Uzbekistan’s ability to turn natural resources into industrial capabilities will be tested.
Energy and Digital Technology Are Part of the Same Challenge
Another priority is modernising the energy system, including renewable generation and energy storage. For a fast-growing economy this is not a secondary concern. New factories, data centres and urban infrastructure increase electricity demand. Unreliable supply can undermine otherwise attractive tax incentives and investment terms.
Uzbekistan is also seeking cooperation on artificial intelligence, digital applications and data centres. The combination is logical: digital infrastructure needs dependable energy, while modern power systems benefit from data analysis, forecasting and sophisticated management tools. Yet importing technology alone does not create a domestic innovation economy.
That requires university programmes, local engineering teams, access for smaller businesses and demand from domestic manufacturers. Without these foundations, digitalisation could remain a collection of isolated projects rather than a driver of productivity.
What Is Changing in US–Uzbek Economic Relations?
The talks suggest a gradual shift from individual commercial transactions towards a more institutionalised partnership. The council brings together political support, specific companies and project coordination. Tashkent has also proposed a long-term trade, investment and technology cooperation programme extending to 2035.
But the durability of this framework will not be determined by the number of official visits. It will depend on business profitability, transparent competition and the consistency of domestic reforms. Even with government support, American companies will make commercial decisions. Uzbekistan must therefore compete for investment while continuing to improve its institutions.
Why Does This Matter for Central Asia?
The regional implications may ultimately be wider than the bilateral relationship. C5+1 provides a forum for Washington and all five Central Asian governments to address connectivity, energy and critical minerals. Yet the region’s economies differ considerably in structure, market size and investment needs.
Kazakhstan offers a larger resource and energy base as well as important Caspian transport links. Uzbekistan combines a substantial population with a growing domestic market and opportunities in manufacturing. Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan may attract interest in hydropower, infrastructure and selected mineral projects. Turkmenistan has considerable energy potential, although investor access remains more restricted.
These differences create both competition for capital and opportunities for cooperation. Minerals from one country could be processed in another, with finished goods reaching external markets through neighbouring transport corridors. Such a model requires compatible standards, customs procedures and energy infrastructure. Without coordination, major investments may remain isolated national ventures.
Greater American engagement should not automatically be interpreted as a replacement for ties with China, Russia or the European Union. For Central Asian economies, diversifying partners is generally more practical than substituting one major relationship for another. More sources of finance, technology and market access can increase room for economic manoeuvre — provided regional governments retain the ability to set their own priorities.
What Comes Next?
The Samarkand agreements should not yet be described as a completed investment breakthrough. They establish a pipeline of opportunities and signal political willingness to pursue them. The next phase must involve financing decisions, operating facilities and durable commercial relationships.
If critical-mineral projects lead to local processing, energy investment improves reliability and digital initiatives develop domestic expertise, the partnership could become one driver of Uzbekistan’s structural modernisation. If most initiatives produce only equipment imports and additional raw-material exports, the long-term benefits will be considerably smaller.
For Washington, Samarkand offers another channel into Central Asia’s economy. For Tashkent, it provides a chance to attract capital and technology without depending on a single outside partner. For the wider region, it illustrates a deeper transformation: Central Asia is increasingly becoming not merely a transit and extraction space, but a place where new manufacturing, investment and trading relationships can emerge.
Markus Friedrich Schneider — independent expert, analyst specializing in the economies of Central Asian countries, contributor to EUobserver.

articles.title: Citibank Kazakhstan Chairperson Sees Opportunities for U.S.-Central Asia Collaboration - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: Citibank Kazakhstan Chairperson Sees Opportunities for U.S.-Central Asia Collaboration  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
Foreign investors are looking outside Kazakhstan’s oil and gas sector. But turning that interest into investment will require predictable regulations and stronger cross-border connections, according to Saule Zhakayeva, chairperson of Citibank Kazakhstan’s management board and president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Kazakhstan (AmCham).
Citi has operated in Kazakhstan since 1994, when it opened a representative office in Almaty. In an interview with The Times of Central Asia, Zhakayeva discussed the country’s investment climate and its role as a regional business hub. She also addressed the future of economic relations between the United States and Kazakhstan.
TCA: How is foreign investor interest in Central Asia evolving, and which of Kazakhstan’s strengths are already translating into investment? Where do you see the strongest commercial opportunities over the next three to five years, and what would help turn untapped potential into committed capital?
Zhakayeva: Investors today are looking for markets that combine economic stability, access to natural resources, strategic geography, and long-term growth potential. Kazakhstan offers each of these attributes. The country has established itself as the largest economy in Central Asia, maintains a relatively strong institutional framework, and continues to pursue reforms aimed at improving the investment climate.
Most notably, investor interest is becoming increasingly diversified. Historically, foreign investment was concentrated primarily in oil and gas. Today, we see growing interest in transportation and logistics, renewable energy, critical minerals, digital infrastructure, financial services, manufacturing, and data-related investments.
This growing interest is also reflected in the increasing level of engagement between international investors and Kazakhstan. As President of the American Chamber of Commerce in Kazakhstan, I have seen firsthand the strong momentum in U.S.-Kazakhstan business relations. Throughout 2026, Kazakhstan has hosted a growing number of high-level business engagements involving senior representatives of American companies and institutions, including the U.S. Chamber of Commerce Business Mission to Kazakhstan and other executive-level dialogues focused on investment, trade, digital transformation, energy, and infrastructure.
AmCham Kazakhstan also led its first business delegation to Washington, D.C., bringing member companies together to strengthen bilateral economic ties, promote Kazakhstan’s investment opportunities, and advocate for deeper economic cooperation. These activities underscore the growing recognition of Kazakhstan and Central Asia as strategically important destinations for long-term investment and commercial cooperation.
More importantly, they are beginning to translate into tangible outcomes. For example, in 2026, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation announced plans to explore up to $700 million in financing opportunities to support the development of Kazakhstan’s critical minerals sector.
Kazakhstan’s location at the crossroads of Europe and Asia has become increasingly important as global companies diversify supply chains and seek alternative trade routes. The development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route is further strengthening Kazakhstan’s role in regional and global commerce, creating opportunities far beyond traditional sectors. Similar dynamics are being observed across the region, where alternative trade routes, logistics investments, and infrastructure development are becoming increasingly important to global investors.
We are also seeing growing international interest in strategic sectors linked to global energy security and the energy transition. Kazakhstan’s role as a major producer of uranium and its potential in critical minerals, renewable energy, and emerging green-energy value chains are attracting increasing international attention. These sectors are becoming increasingly important as governments and companies seek to diversify supply chains and secure access to strategic resources.
Looking ahead over the next three to five years, I believe the strongest opportunities will emerge in infrastructure, transport and logistics, the energy transition, critical minerals, digital economy initiatives, and sectors supporting regional trade.
To translate interest into committed capital, investors continue to value predictability. Continued progress in regulatory transparency, efficient infrastructure development, human capital, and cross-border connectivity will further strengthen Kazakhstan’s competitiveness.
TCA: Kazakhstan has faced repeated external shocks, including recent disruptions affecting global trade routes and financial markets. How do you assess its resilience, particularly in light of the recent sovereign rating upgrade to BBB by S&P Global Ratings and the country’s substantial financial buffers? Looking ahead, where do you see the main vulnerabilities, and what practical steps should companies take to mitigate financial and supply-chain risks?
Zhakayeva: Kazakhstan has demonstrated considerable resilience in navigating successive external shocks. Its macroeconomic fundamentals remain relatively strong, supported by substantial sovereign financial reserves, prudent fiscal management, and a diversified banking sector.
The recent upgrade of Kazakhstan’s sovereign credit rating to BBB by S&P is a significant milestone. Sovereign ratings are closely monitored by global investors because they provide an independent assessment of a country’s creditworthiness, policy credibility, and capacity to meet its financial obligations. The upgrade reflects confidence in Kazakhstan’s economic management, institutional framework, external balance sheet, and ability to maintain stability despite a challenging global environment.
We have observed this progress firsthand. Citi has served as an adviser to the Government of Kazakhstan on sovereign ratings since 2019, working closely with economic authorities to support engagement with international rating agencies and investors. During this period, Kazakhstan has achieved six sovereign rating upgrades, reflecting continued improvements in economic fundamentals, governance, and policy credibility. Today, Citi is also supporting discussions around a medium-term roadmap aimed at further strengthening Kazakhstan’s sovereign credit profile over time.
From an investment perspective, a stronger sovereign rating can help improve investor confidence, support access to international capital markets, and contribute to lower financing costs over time for both the public and private sectors. Combined with Kazakhstan’s substantial sovereign assets and financial buffers, it reinforces the country’s position as one of the stronger investment-grade markets in the region.
Investor engagement is equally important. As a committed financial partner to Kazakhstan for more than 30 years, Citi continues to help connect the country with global capital markets and international investors. Through investor forums, roadshows, and strategic dialogues in major financial centers such as New York and London, we help showcase Kazakhstan’s economic progress, reform agenda, and long-term investment potential to the global investment community.
At the same time, resilience today does not mean immunity. Businesses operate in an environment characterized by volatile commodity prices, changing trade patterns, geopolitical uncertainty, and fluctuating financial conditions. The most successful companies are responding by focusing on diversification. One of the key lessons emerging globally is that no company or country can rely on a single market, supplier, financing source, or trade route. Recent disruptions have reinforced the importance of building multiple channels for sourcing, logistics, and market access. Similar observations have been made regarding global supply chains and trade routes, where organizations increasingly seek alternatives rather than depending on a single corridor.
From a practical standpoint, companies should prioritize active foreign exchange risk management and hedging programs; diversification of funding sources and financing tenors; supply chain mapping and contingency planning; digital visibility across procurement and logistics networks; scenario planning to prepare for external disruptions.
Resilience is no longer simply about absorbing shocks. It is about maintaining strategic flexibility and being able to adapt quickly as circumstances evolve.

A growing number of international companies are evaluating Kazakhstan as a base from which to serve Central Asia and neighboring markets. Several factors are driving this trend.

articles.title: The end of post-Soviet unity? Russian influence and Armenia’s strategic dilemmas - Defence24.com
articles.summary: The end of post-Soviet unity? Russian influence and Armenia’s strategic dilemmas  Defence24.com
articles.full_text:
The Commonwealth of Independent States is an organisation established in the 1990s following the collapse of the Soviet Union. It was created as a platform for cooperation among the former Soviet republics. In its early years, the CIS played a key role in stabilising the region after the dissolution of the Soviet Union. The organisation coordinated the division of Soviet assets, the management of the strategic nuclear arsenal, and issues related to the transit of energy resources. The Commonwealth also established a framework for resolving disputes between member states peacefully. Over time, however, many of these functions ceased to be carried out effectively.
Conflicts between the organisation’s members and Russia’s imperial policy are among the reasons why the CIS is losing its significance. The dispute between Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, armed clashes between Armenia and Azerbaijan, and Russia’s wars against Georgia and Ukraine—both former members of the organisation—have seriously called into question the practical value of its existence. For Russia, the CIS is one of the instruments of geopolitical, economic and propaganda influence. For the Kremlin, the organisation is a mechanism for keeping the former Soviet republics within its exclusive sphere of influence.
Russia dominates CIS structures militarily and economically. It uses trade agreements within the bloc to make smaller states—such as Armenia, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan—dependent on its markets, energy supplies (gas and oil) and remittances sent by migrant workers. At CIS summits, Vladimir Putin regularly calls for the “removal of trade barriers”, which in practice means opening these countries’ markets further to Russian capital and limiting their economic sovereignty. For the Kremlin, the CIS is an invaluable propaganda tool on the international stage. By organising regular summits attended by the leaders of post-Soviet states, Russia can demonstrate—particularly in the face of Western sanctions imposed after its invasion of Ukraine—that it is not isolated and still leads a powerful bloc of countries. This helps legitimise Russia’s imperial policy.
Russia presents itself as the sole and ultimate arbiter in regional conflicts within the CIS, including the border disputes between Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan and relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan. Rather than pursuing lasting solutions, Moscow often preserves the status quo or employs a “divide and rule” strategy, offering military support or diplomatic mediation in exchange for the parties’ political loyalty.
How does Armenia see its place in this arrangement? Armenia regards the CIS as a relatively neutral body. Given its flexibility and limited institutional formalisation, Yerevan views the organisation as a platform for dialogue and meetings with other leaders from the former Soviet Union. Armenia has frozen its participation in another Russian-led organisation, the Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO), because it failed to fulfil its obligation to assist Armenia in 2022, during Azerbaijan’s attack on Armenia’s internationally recognised territory. Yerevan remains a member of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), an organisation established in 2014. The EAEU allows the free movement of goods, services, capital and labour. Remaining a member is economically beneficial for Armenia. The Union’s rules ensure the free movement of goods and allow Armenia to purchase crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas at preferential prices.
However, disputes between Russia and Armenia within the Union have become increasingly frequent.
Moscow has imposed restrictions on imports of various Armenian goods, citing, among other things, alleged sanitary issues.
The restrictions have affected alcoholic beverages, dairy products, flowers and foodstuffs.
Russia has also used the threat of completely cutting off gas and oil supplies to Armenia as a means of pressure.
The dispute has intensified because of Armenia’s aspirations to join the European Union and the Nikol Pashinyan-led Armenian government’s criticism of the Kremlin’s policy.
Armenia takes a pragmatic and flexible approach to its relations with Russian-led structures, seeking cooperation wherever it serves its interests.
It is, however, becoming increasingly difficult.
In connection with its plans to submit a formal application for EU membership, Armenia may face an important choice between the “East” and the “West”.
As part of the ongoing debate in Armenia about beginning the EU integration process, Nikol Pashinyan has proposed a referendum in which citizens could express whether they support the idea of integration with the EU.
The timing of such a referendum remains distant and difficult to determine, but the very idea of joining Western structures has drawn criticism from the Kremlin.
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin issued what amounted to an ultimatum to Yerevan, demanding a declaration on the referendum by December 2026.
Prime Minister Pashinyan rejected this pressure, maintaining his proposed sequence: first a formal application and candidate status, and only then a nationwide referendum.

Tensions between Yerevan and Moscow appear likely to escalate further. As Armenia deepens its integration with Western countries, Russia will use additional forms of pressure. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly declared an end to Armenia’s policy of “relying on Russia” and announced a multi-vector foreign policy based on cooperation with a range of different partners.
About the Author:
Dominik Lebioda is a graduate of the University of Łódź with a master’s degree in international relations. His main research interests include the South Caucasus—particularly Armenia—Armenia’s foreign policy, geopolitical rivalry in the post-Soviet space, and international cooperation among cities and regions.

articles.title: Uzbekistan Announces $12 Billion in Agreements During Marco Rubio’s Visit - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: Uzbekistan Announces $12 Billion in Agreements During Marco Rubio’s Visit  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
Uzbekistan has announced 54 agreements covering trade, investment, and technological cooperation during U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit to Samarkand. The agreements are worth a total of $12 billion, according to Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade.
The agreements were announced at the second meeting of the Uzbekistan–U.S. Business and Investment Council on October 19. Rubio also met President Shavkat Mirziyoyev that day.
The ministry said the agreements cover transport and energy infrastructure, critical minerals, finance, digital technologies, agriculture, healthcare, and education. Rubio’s visit coincided with a C5+1 ministerial meeting, bringing together the United States and the five Central Asian countries.
The Uzbek ministry stated that more than 400 business representatives participated in the program, including over 100 from the United States, 100 from other Central Asian countries, and 200 from Uzbekistan. It did not specify how much of the announced $12 billion has secured financing and how much remains at the planning stage.
Several international companies were named in the agreements announced during the visit.
According to the announced arrangements, cooperation with Wabtec is focused on localizing the production of railway equipment and components. Agreements involving ReElement Technologies, Traxys, and Trafigura cover mineral exploration, development, technological cooperation, and supplies.
Other announced projects involve satellite communications with Amazon Leo, medical technologies with GE HealthCare, and agricultural efficiency with Valmont Industries.
Speaking to reporters in Samarkand on October 19, Rubio said the visit was expected to produce concrete commercial results.
“I think we’ll have some concrete deals to announce, meaning companies that are going to be doing business here that are being welcomed here and that are excited about doing business here,” Rubio said.
He emphasized that the agreements should be viewed as the beginning of a broader economic relationship.
“I also think that’s just the foundation that we intend to build on. We want to do more. This is not the end. This is the beginning,” he said.
In their joint statement, the C5+1 governments supported expanding mineral processing and higher-value production within Central Asia. They also backed further development of the Trans-Caspian Trade Route and closer regional economic integration.
The visit also marked the launch of the Enhanced Strategic Partnership Dialogue and Uzbekistan’s signing of the Artemis Accords on peaceful space exploration.
From Investment Announcements to Projects
In an interview with The Times of Central Asia (TCA), political analyst Abduvali Soyibnazarov described Rubio’s visit and the C5+1 meeting as a potentially important stage in Washington’s relations with Central Asia.
Recalling the first C5+1 ministerial meeting, attended by then-U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry in Samarkand in November 2015, Soyibnazarov said the agenda has changed considerably over the past decade, with investment, critical minerals, advanced technologies, and new trade routes moving to the forefront. The analyst argued that Uzbekistan’s main measure of success should not be the number of memorandums signed, but how many projects ultimately secure financing and move forward.
Uzbekistan’s investment minister, Laziz Kudratov, put the country’s portfolio of commercial agreements with the United States at $35 billion in a September interview. He said projects worth $7 billion had been implemented and completed. It is unclear whether the $12 billion announced during Rubio’s visit forms part of that existing portfolio.
Critical Minerals and Industrial Development
Critical mineral extraction and processing have emerged as major areas of potential cooperation between the United States and Uzbekistan. The minerals talks build on a bilateral memorandum on critical minerals supply chains signed in February, covering both mining and processing.
Washington is seeking to diversify supplies of materials used in advanced technologies and reduce its dependence on China. For Uzbekistan, Soyibnazarov said, the challenge is to use American commercial interest not only to increase mineral exports, but to develop domestic processing industries.
The analyst pointed to Uzbekistan’s $4.2 billion national program for critical minerals development in 2026–2030, which aims to expand processing capacity within the country. In Soyibnazarov’s assessment, investment in processing plants, laboratories, and finished-product manufacturing could help Uzbekistan capture more value from its mineral resources, strengthen its industrial base, and create skilled jobs.
Economist Norpulat Daniyarov told TCA that U.S. interest in Central Asia extends beyond mineral extraction.
“The United States is prioritizing Central Asia’s critical minerals and logistics sectors,” Daniyarov said. “In Uzbekistan, financial sector development will also be important, while energy presents significant opportunities for U.S. companies in Turkmenistan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.”
Daniyarov stated that critical minerals are important to Washington not only because of their commercial value, but because they are essential to artificial intelligence, electric vehicles, and other advanced technologies.
Finance and New Trade Routes
Financial cooperation is another major component of the announced agreements.
Arrangements involving Franklin Templeton, Oppenheimer & Co., Citigroup, and BlackRock are intended to help Uzbek companies access international capital markets, attract institutional investors, and finance infrastructure projects.
BlackRock is also helping develop the structure of the Tashkent International Financial Centre. Daniyarov said Uzbekistan needs both foreign investment and technical expertise to modernize its banking sector. The economist also highlighted transport infrastructure. In his assessment, Russia’s war in Ukraine, sanctions affecting Russia and Iran, and efforts to diversify trade routes have increased the importance of alternative overland connections.
“The United States and the European Union need reliable land trade routes to Asia that bypass Russia,” Daniyarov said.
Uzbekistan, however, relies on several transit routes, including connections through Iran. Consequently, Tashkent’s and Washington’s logistics interests do not always fully coincide. Changes in sanctions and transit conditions can affect shipping costs and access to international markets.
One alternative is the Middle Corridor, which connects Central Asia across the Caspian Sea to the South Caucasus and Europe. Further development of this route could expand Uzbekistan’s transport options and reduce dependence on a limited number of transit partners.
Balancing U.S., Chinese, and Russian Interests
Daniyarov believes that an expanded U.S. economic presence could give Central Asian countries greater opportunities to diversify their international partnerships. Russia remains an important trade and economic partner for the region, while China has significantly expanded its presence over the past 10 to 15 years through investment, infrastructure projects, and the Belt and Road Initiative.
Daniyarov argued that Central Asian governments should use growing U.S. interest to attract capital into sectors beyond raw material extraction.
“Central Asian countries should seize this opportunity to attract U.S. investment, particularly in artificial intelligence, data centers, advanced technologies, energy and financial sector development,” he said.
The economist also proposed greater coordination between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan in attracting investment in rare earth and other critical minerals.
“If countries compete individually to export raw materials, the region may lose leverage and capture only limited value,” Daniyarov warned.
In his view, a coordinated approach could strengthen Central Asian countries’ negotiating positions when seeking technology transfers and investment in mineral processing, artificial intelligence, and data centers.
Jackson-Vanik and the Trade Relationship
Rubio’s visit also renewed attention to the Jackson-Vanik amendment, a Cold War-era U.S. trade restriction that remains formally applicable to Uzbekistan. Repealing the amendment would help establish permanent normal trade relations between the two countries. The decision, however, rests with the U.S. Congress.
During the press conference in Samarkand, reporters asked Rubio why the amendment had not yet been repealed.
“You’ll have to ask Congress,” he responded. “We are in favor of repealing it.”
Rubio stated that he had supported its repeal during his confirmation hearing and said the administration had asked lawmakers to act.
“Congress just hasn’t gotten around to it, but we hope that they will,” he added.
Commenting on the issue for TCA, Soyibnazarov emphasized that repealing Jackson-Vanik cannot be achieved through a single diplomatic visit. He argued that Uzbekistan should seek a clear political commitment from the U.S. administration to make repeal a legislative priority.
The amendment also has implications for Uzbekistan’s accession to the World Trade Organization. Although bilateral WTO accession negotiations with Washington have been completed, a separate decision by U.S. lawmakers remains necessary to establish permanent normal trade relations.
Technology Partnerships and Strategic Choices
Soyibnazarov believes that expanding cooperation with Washington presents Tashkent with the challenge of maintaining independence in its choice of technological partners. articles.title: Korybko To Bordachev: The Threat Posed By ISIS-K Will Keep Russia & Central Asia Close - Howl.link
articles.summary: Korybko To Bordachev: The Threat Posed By ISIS-K Will Keep Russia & Central Asia Close  Howl.link
articles.full_text:
Valdai Club Programme Director Timofei Bordachev published a piece at Vzglyad about how “Russia is assessing old and new threats in Central Asia.” He touched upon their shared interests in thwarting the threat posed by ISIS-K in Afghanistan and their stakes in Iran’s resilience to US-Israeli pressure before hinting that the Central Asian Republics (CARs) might leverage their geostrategic location in the escalating Sino-US rivalry. That could in turn lead to the reduction of Russian influence.
According to him, “the seas around Asia and Eurasia will be a zone of crisis, while the land will be a space of prosperity. Partly for this reason, our friends and allies in the region now feel relatively confident about their own future. And this confidence can sometimes appear as overconfidence, a departure from the traditional policy of special bilateral relations with Russia.” Bordachev nevertheless predicted that the CARs will remain practical in their dealings with Russia and vice versa. Afghanistan is the reason why.
He cited Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov’s speech at a recent multilateral event in Moscow on security in Central Asia and Afghanistan to raise readers’ awareness of the threats posed by ISIS-K in Afghanistan such as arms and drug smuggling as well as terrorism. Bordachev didn’t mention it, but Lavrov also warned that “a significant presence of terrorist and extremist groups, along with their training camps and strongholds, remains in Afghan areas bordering Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan.”
Russia’s potential arming of the Taliban against ISIS-K is only one part of a three-part solution for thwarting this threat. The other two are for Pakistan to cut off the flow of ammo, arms, and terrorists to Afghanistan, which leading Russian officials have strongly hinted is a problem as documented here but is beyond the Kremlin’s ability to meaningfully influence, and closer security coordination with the CARs. The only one of Afghanistan’s neighbors that’s part of the Russian-led CSTO is Tajikistan, however.
Therefore, a combination of bilateral and multilateral CSTO-led security cooperation is required with Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan, the first of which is the region’s most populous country whose people have a well-known susceptibility to fundamentalism and unrest while the second’s sparsely populated border could be relatively easy for ISIS-K to overrun unless it’s comprehensively fortified and monitored. Such Afghan-emanating threats from ISIS-K are expected to remain even if the group is formally crushed.
Neither the US, China, nor aspiring regional hegemon Turkiye have anywhere near Russia’s capability to assist the CARs with thwarting these threats, ergo why they’re expected to remain close as a result. The gradual transformation of last year’s proposed “Central Asian Community” (CAC) into an ASEAN-like regional bloc, which now includes Azerbaijan, could further facilitate their shared anti-terrorist efforts. It would also aid regional economic integration and thus make the CARs better partners for Afghanistan.
In the absence of progress on resolving Pakistan’s role in Afghanistan’s security challenges, which was never seriously expected, Russia will accordingly redouble its security-driven rapprochement with the Taliban and related security-driven ties with the CARs/CAC for jointly thwarting ISIS-K’s threats. Therefore, no matter whatever strides America, China, or aspiring regional hegemon Turkiye may make in the region, the CARs’ closest ally should remain Russia, whose interests they’re unlikely to go against.

articles.title: Kazakhstan - Nomadic, Turkic, Diverse - Britannica
articles.summary: Kazakhstan - Nomadic, Turkic, Diverse  Britannica
articles.full_text:
Ethnic groups
Fewer than one-fifth of the more than eight million ethnic Kazakhs live outside Kazakhstan, mainly in Uzbekistan and Russia. During the 19th century about 400,000 Russians flooded into Kazakhstan, and these were supplemented by about 1,000,000 Slavs, Germans, Jews, and others who immigrated to the region during the first third of the 20th century. The immigrants crowded Kazakhs off the best pastures and watered lands, rendering many tribes destitute. Another large influx of Slavs occurred from 1954 to 1956 as a result of the Virgin and Idle Lands project, initiated by the Soviet premier Nikita Khrushchev, himself a Slav. This project drew thousands of Russians and Ukrainians into the rich agricultural lands of northern Kazakhstan. By 1989, however, Kazakhs slightly outnumbered Russians.
News •
In the early years of independence, significant numbers of ethnic Russians in Kazakhstan emigrated to Russia. This emigration, along with a return to the country of ethnic Kazakhs, changed the demographic makeup of Kazakhstan: by the mid-1990s the Kazakh proportion was approaching half the total population, while that for the Russians was closer to one-third.
The trend persisted into the 21st century, and by the 2020s the Kazakh population was more than two-thirds of the country’s total population while the Russian community represented less than one-sixth. Other ethnic groups in Kazakhstan include Uzbeks, Uyghurs, and Tajiks, along with Ukrainians, Germans, Tatars, and Koreans.
Although Slavs were more numerous than Kazakhs in urban areas at the beginning of Kazakhstan’s independence, the proportion of Kazakhs to Slavs has steadily increased. In 2025 Kazakhs constituted nearly two-thirds of the population of Almaty, the country’s largest city. According to the 1999 census, they constituted less than two-fifths of the population while Russians comprised nearly half.
Languages
Kazakhs speak a Turkic language of the Northwest or Kipchak (Qipchaq) group. Russian, an official language, functions widely alongside Kazakh, which is the state language. Russian is the most widely understood language in the country.
Religion
The Kazakhs are a nominally Muslim people. During much of their long nomadic period, the Kazakhs’ adherence to Islam remained informal and permissive. When they moved into settlements or sent their children to towns such as Sterlitamak or Bukhara for an education, that situation changed. There, young Kazakhs entered Muslim maktabs and madrasahs, where religion supplied the main subjects and ideology. Thus, the younger generation of intellectuals turned into urban-style Muslims before the Soviet communists took over in the early 1920s. Thereafter, the authorities actively suppressed or discouraged religious life in Kazakhstan until the U.S.S.R. disintegrated. Since independence, Kazakhs generally have enjoyed freedom of religion. About one-fourth of the population is Eastern Orthodox.
Settlement patterns
More than three-fifths the population is considered urban, while less than two-fifths of the population is rural. The extremely wide dispersion of population in Kazakhstan is reflected in the large number of small settlements. Although Kazakhstan is the ninth largest country in the world in terms of land mass, fewer than 120 settlements fell into the category of city or town in 2025. More than 6,000 settlements were auyls (small farm villages).
Kazakhstan’s distinct regional patterns of settlement depend in part on its varied ethnic makeup. Slavs—Russians, Ukrainians, and Belarusians—largely populate the northern plains, where they congregate in large villages that originally served as the centers of collective and state farms. These populated oases are separated by wheat fields or, in the more arid plains to the south, by semideserts and deserts where sheep breeders live in temporary quarters, usually yurts (round tents with sturdy pole frames covered by heavy felt).
Kazakh nomads formerly obtained their schooling and manufactured goods from Russian towns such as Troitsk, Orenburg, and Omsk, or, in the south, from the ancient cities of Transoxania, the Fergana Valley, and eastern Turkistan. After the Russian conquest established military governors and administrators in Alma-Ata (now Almaty), Uralsk (Oral), Yaik, and elsewhere, Kazakhstan began in the 19th century to develop its own cities. Qarağandy (Karaganda), Öskemen (Ust-Kamenogorsk), and Rudnyi, which are typical Soviet planned towns, have straight, wide streets and multistoried buildings and accommodate industry around their fringes.
Demographic trends
The population of Kazakhstan is young. About half the population is under age 30, and more than one-fourth is under the age of 15. The birth and death rates are roughly equal to the global average. Life expectancy for men is 69 years, though life expectancy for women is much higher, at 78.
Economy
Kazakhstan possesses abundant natural resources. Its major exports include agricultural products, raw materials, chemical products, and manufactured goods. Privatization of state-owned industries was undertaken during the 1990s. In 1994 Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Kyrgyzstan formed an economic union, later joined in 1998 by Tajikistan, that enabled free movement of labor and capital among the countries and established coordinated economic policies. The union gradually gave way to what became the Eurasian Economic Union, consisting of Kazakhstan, Russia, Belarus, Armenia, and Kyrgyzstan.
Resources
Kazakhstan is the world’s leading producer of uranium, supplying more than two-fifths of the global output by the early 2020s. Despite some hesitancy to develop a nuclear industry—Kazakhstan was the site of hundreds of nuclear tests during the Soviet era—the construction of nuclear power plants was approved in a referendum in 2024. A Russian company began work on the first nuclear power plant in 2025, and a second plant was slated to be built by a Chinese company.
A large deposit of rare-earth metals, estimated to be as much as 20 million tons, was discovered in Qarağandy province in 2025; extraction is expected in the mid-to-late 2030s. Other important mineral resources include copper in the central areas and in Aqtöbe province; lead, zinc, and silver in the Rudnyi Altai area and the Dzungarian Alatau and Qaratau (Karatau) spurs; tungsten and tin in the Kalba (Kalbinsky) Ridge and southern Altai; chromite, nickel, and cobalt in Mugaljar; titanium, manganese, and antimony in the central regions; vanadium in the south; and gold in the north and east. Much iron ore comes from Qarağandy and Qostanai (Kustanay), and coal from the Qarağandy, Torğai (Turgay), Ekıbastūz, and Maikuben basins. In 1993 Kazakhstan finalized a contract with the Chevron Corporation to exploit the reserves of the Tengiz oil field, marking the world’s largest oil strike in two decades. Other major oil fields include Karachaganak, which began operation in the late Soviet era, and Kashagan, whose development in the early 21st century made it the largest oil field outside the Middle East.
Agriculture
Farming occupies some one-fifth of the labor force, largely the Kazakh portion plus the Slavic wheat farmers of northern Kazakhstan. Kazakhs raise sheep, goats, cattle, and swine. The country produces cereal crops, potatoes, vegetables, melons and other fruits, sugar beets, and rice, as well as fodder and industrial crops. Nuclear contamination of soils near Semei—the result of Soviet weapons testing—has hindered agricultural development in the northeast.
Industry
Industry constitutes a prominent sector of the Kazakh economy, but it employs fewer than one-tenth of the indigenous Kazakhs. Manufacturing industries employing primarily Russian and Ukrainian workers produce cast iron, rolled steel, cement, chemical fertilizer, and consumer goods. Plants in Temirtau and Qarağandy produce steel. The country, with its nonferrous metallurgy concentrated in the east, is a major lead and copper producer. Kazakhstan’s fuel production has increased with the extraction of coal from the Qarağandy and Ekıbastūz basins.
Meatpacking plants operate in many areas, but creameries exist chiefly in areas settled by Slavs in the north and east. Sugar refineries are located in the south in the Taldyqorğan (Taldy-Kurgan) and Almaty areas. Fruit and vegetable canning, grain milling, brewing, and wine making are among the light industries. Synthetic fibers come from a factory at Qarağandy and pharmaceuticals from a plant in Shymkent (Şymkent).
Trade
Kazakhstan’s main export commodities include oil and natural gas, various metals, and chemicals. Its primary export destinations are Italy, China, Russia, and the Netherlands. Imports include machinery, metal and chemical products, and foodstuffs. Russia and China are its main sources of imports.
Transportation
Railways carry most of the freight going long distances. The Trans-Siberian, South Siberian, and Kazakh (formerly Turkistan-Siberian) trunk lines cross Kazakhstan east to west, and the Orenburg line extends as far as Tashkent in the south. Air transport carries the bulk of passenger traffic, both domestic and regional. The international airport at Almaty offers service to Frankfurt (Germany), Istanbul, and other cities. The next stage will depend on whether businesses can turn these established trade flows into new supply contracts, distribution networks and long-term investment projects. This article explains these development dynamics and is essential reading for anyone involved in Russian and ASEAN affairs.
The immediate Russian trade and investment opportunities are visible across Southeast Asia. Vietnam recorded US$4.77 billion in bilateral trade with Russia in 2025, while Indonesia’s trade approached US$5 billion. On October 14, he met Russian Minister of Science and Higher Education Valery Falkov and members of the ASEAN Committee in Moscow. Its 11 areas are trade and investment, digital transformation, science and technology, transport, agriculture, energy, mining, climate change, the circular economy, tourism and the creative economy. Businesses need workable customs procedures, reliable payments, clear technical requirements, transport links and commercially viable contracts. The Vietnam-EAEU Free Trade Agreement provides an existing route for tariff reductions and market access.
