From holding meetings with the Gulf Cooperation Council members and bilateral meetings with the Foreign Ministers of Bahrain, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, the Russian Foreign Minister, Sergey Lavrov arrived in Tehran to hold discussions with Masoud Pezeshkian, the Iranian President, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, and Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei.
At the same time, Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin, held talks with Iranian First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref in Dushanbe, Tajikistan. Lavrov’s mission appears to have been diplomacy based, looking at ways to prevent further conflict in the Middle East and broker some agreements between Iran and especially Saudi Arabia, where Iran has attacked US air force bases. Mishustin’s meetings appear to have been more trade and investment related. We will deal with these separately as follows:
Lavrov’s Meetings With Pezeshkian
The discussions conveyed the views of GCC members – who Lavrov had met the day before and addressed the situation in the Gulf region and ways to resolve the international crisis. They also discussed further steps to strengthen coordination within the United Nations and expand cooperation through BRICS, the SCO, and the EAEU.
President Pezeshkian urged faster implementation of existing joint agreements, highlighting energy, transportation, trade, and power plant infrastructure. Lavrov stressed Russia and Iran’s alignment on global issues and the need for ongoing diplomatic talks. and noted that Moscow expects President Pezeshkian to attend the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit scheduled in Moscow next week.
Discussions focused heavily on resolving the “acute international crisis” in the Middle East. Lavrov emphasized that Russia’s diplomatic efforts at the United Nations are aimed at preventing a larger-scale war, offering Moscow’s continued assistance to facilitate a peaceful resolution.
Much of these discussions would have been security related and not open for public disbursement.
Lavrov’s Meetings With Araghchi
This was the fourth meeting between the two countries’ foreign ministers this year, in addition to 14 telephone conversations. The ministers reviewed the implementation of agreements reached during talks between President of Russia Vladimir Putin and President Pezeshkian on September 1, with particular attention paid to current issues in trade, economic and investment cooperation, as well as the implementation of major joint projects in the transport, logistics and energy sectors.
The ministers addressed ongoing insecurity in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. Araghchi blamed U.S. and Israeli military aggression for the tensions, while Lavrov called for a return to conditions that secure freedom of navigation. Despite international pressure, Lavrov made it clear that Russia will not abandon its joint economic, energy, transport, and investment agreements with Tehran, and detailed that Russia is continuing to provide direct humanitarian aid to Iran, including shipments of essential medicines and food supplies.
Lavrov said that “Despite the challenging situation, which has repeatedly been mentioned, Russia has no intention to abandon the implementation of economic and investment agreements with Iran. Great prospects are opening up in hydrocarbon extraction and transportation. Russia’s contractor is continuing engineering surveys along the route of the future Rasht-Astara railway line project and will begin construction as soon as the Iranian side completes the processing of necessary documents.”
The meeting underscored a strengthening comprehensive strategic partnership rooted in a mutual defense and threat-countering pact signed in 2025. Araghchi remarked that “never in our history have Iran and Russia worked as closely as now”.
Lavrov’s Meetings With Rezaei
Lavrov also held talks with Major-General Mohsen Rezaei, the Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council. Rezaei emphasized that Tehran is fully resolved to solidify and expand its long-term strategic and bilateral relations with Moscow, and noted that under the shifting regional circumstances, ongoing stability and security in the Middle East depend heavily on multilateral cooperation among regional countries, free from foreign coercion.
They reviewed joint economic initiatives, specifically highlighting the completion of strategic transport corridors as key drivers for regional stability and economic development, while Lavrov reaffirmed Russia’s robust support for Iran’s positions and initiatives across international forums, including the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). Russia is heavily involved in developing Iran’s nuclear energy sector. Lavrov mentioned that Russian specialists are gradually returning to the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant, which was bombed by US aircraft earlier this year. Moscow and Tehran are looking to build eight new NPP in Iran in the coming years as the country seeks to modernise its energy supplies. The NPP technology being considered cannot be repurposed to manufacture nuclear weapons.
Mishustin’s Meetings With Aref
Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin, who has arrived in Tajikistan to attend a meeting of prime ministers from Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) member countries, held talks with Iranian First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref also on October 19. The Russian delegation also included Deputy Prime Minister Alexey Overchuk, Minister of Economic Development Maxim Reshetnikov, Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko, Deputy Energy Minister Yevgeny Grabchak, and Deputy Finance Minister Alexey Sazanov.
They also discussed the construction of new reactors at the Bushehr NPP, as well as outstanding issues relating to the Racht-Astara railway, a key link in the western corridor of the INSTC. While Lavrov stated that Russia was still waiting for Iranian documentation procedures to be completed, Deputy Prime Minister Overchuk revealed that Iran has notified the Russian side about the completion of the buyout of land for the construction of the Rasht-Astara railway section. Overchuk said that “The negotiation participants exchanged opinions. In the first place, the status of implementation of our North-South project, the construction of the section of the future Rasht-Astara railway was discussed. The Iranian side assured us that the land plots have been bought. We expect documentary confirmation of the buyout. The creation of this railway line is already being carried out by the Russian contractor.”
Overchuk added that “Issues concerning construction in the Caspian Sea and transportation in the Caspian Sea, primarily food transportation, were also discussed.”
For his part, Mishustin said that “At the government level, we are prioritizing the expansion of trade and economic cooperation, our trade grew last year and continues increasing despite geopolitical challenges and sanctions” and added that the implementation of the free trade agreement between the Eurasian Economic Union and Iran is yielding positive results.
He said “We are also implementing major joint projects in the energy sector, including the peaceful use of nuclear energy, as well as in industry, transport infrastructure, and agriculture. The North-South Transport Corridor, which connects Eurasia to the Persian Gulf and the Indian Ocean, is being actively developed. This project of regional significance will provide direct access to the growing markets of the Asia-Pacific region and Africa and will facilitate the creation of new production and logistics chains across Eurasia.”
Bilateral trade between Russia and Iran reached about US$5.8 billion in 2025, marking an increase of more than 21% compared to the previous year. Lavrov mentioned that 2026 trade grew by over 10% during the first eight months of 2026.
New Iran-India Rail Route Completed
In related news, Iran has completed a key railway line connecting its southern port of Chabahar with Zahedan near its border with Afghanistan, amid a US blockade of its ports and mounting economic pressure from the West. The 730-km rail link gives Tehran more flexibility to move cargo to neighboring countries from the port, which is being developed by India.
The railway is a key link in the INSTC, with Iran’s broader ambition is to connect its southern ports to transport networks connecting the Caspian Sea and beyond, operationalizing a vast land corridor for market access across Afghanistan, Central Asia, and Russia. It offers an overland trade route bypassing Pakistan to connect the Indian Ocean with Afghanistan, Central Asia, and Russia, and is funded by Iran’s National Development Fund after initial foreign participation stalled due to US sanctions.
The Chabahar route is 40% shorter and 30% less costly than the existing Suez Canal route for moving cargo. The line, which has 39 tunnels, 201 bridges, and 33 stations, is currently undergoing testing and expected to become operational early next year. It can also move about 7 million tons of cargo and 1 million passengers annually.
The route also allows India to bypass Pakistan to access Iranian markets, although sanctions and blockades remain a challenge. However, New Delhi and Tehran are actively engaged in smoothing out customs, logistics, and operational issues to maximize the line’s commercial potential. Former Indian Ambassador to Iran D.P. Srivastava has said ”Central Asia and Russia are closer to India if we take the land routes.”
It also links through to Afghanistan’s rail network to Kabul, which is poised to become a Central Asia transit hub. articles.title: Does Trump’s 60-day tariff waiver really give relief to India? What it means for US trade deal & oil prices - The Times of India
articles.summary: Does Trump’s 60-day tariff waiver really give relief to India? What it means for US trade deal & oil prices  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
What does US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions on Russia and tariffs on countries buying oil from Moscow really mean for India? The US decision to waive the proposed sanctions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 is clearly aimed at securing relief for its own country.
The development comes amid America’s shifting approach to Russian energy. In a separate deal, Russia agreed to release more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel for the US and global markets, with further supplies proposed for subsequent months.
While the US-Russia diesel deal primarily focused on the bilateral US-Russia relations, the tariff waiver is mostly directed to India and China. The threatened 100% tariffs on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas were due to take effect 30 days after the legislation’s approval on September 18.
Also Read | 
The return of Middle East oil: Has Iran lost control of Strait of Hormuz & why are crude prices still up?
What Trump has done
Trump invoked Section 115 of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 to issue the waiver. He certified that it was in the national interest of the US.
"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver is in the national interests of the United States and a report explaining the basis for the certification, consistent with section 115(b) of the Graham Act," Trump said.
The waiver applies to duties under Sections 112 and 113, which authorised tariffs of up to 500% on goods that are imported from Russia and up to 100% on goods from the five largest buyers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas. India and China were among the countries potentially covered by the latter provision.
Trump's sanctions and tariff waiver explained
But, Natalia Katona, Commodity Analyst sees the move as less of a gift to Moscow than an attempt to keep a lid on oil prices.
“Russian crude continued to find buyers despite the tariff threat, effectively the entire November loading programme of Russian export grades has been sold off even though it could’ve been subjected to tariffs,” she tells TOI.
“Enforcing the Lindsey Graham Act would risk disrupting future Russian crude flows and pushing Brent above its current level of around $110 a barrel. With US elections approaching in early November, my reading is that Trump wants to avoid another oil-price shock at all costs,” she says.
What it means for India
For India, the immediate relief is for its crude supply basket and exporters. If India decided to give up Russian crude oil, its single largest supplier would have gone off the table, with no easy replacement amid Middle East tensions. If it continued to buy Russian crude, then the 100% tariffs would have weighed on its exports to the US.
Russian oil supplies to India hit a record high earlier this year when the closure of Strait of Hormuz limited the Middle East crude supplies.
But recently, buying patterns have made a notable shift to the Middle East as supplies through the Strait of Hormuz ease and China begins competing for the same Russian barrels, driving up the cost of oil from Moscow.
Pankaj Srivastava, Senior Vice President, Commodity Market - Oil at Rystad Energy is of the view that India was strategically prepared for the Graham bill, with crude supply from the Middle East rising significantly to approximately 2.5 million bpd in September, while Russian imports declined to around 1.5 million bpd.
The increase in Middle Eastern supply was supported by the continued operation of multiple logistics channels, including the Strait of Hormuz, dark fleet movements, ship-to-ship transfers, alternative Red Sea and Suez Canal routes, and the East-West Pipeline.
“As a result, Middle Eastern crude exports increased to nearly 15 million barrels per day in September, strengthening India's import availability. At the same time, higher insurance and freight costs associated with Black Sea exports, following recent attacks in the region, reduced the competitiveness of Russian crude,” Pankaj Srivastava tells TOI.
According to the expert, with ongoing refinery expansions and strong diesel crack margins supporting exports, the waiver further improves feedstock security for Indian refiners.
“This development is also constructive for global distillate markets and could provide additional support to diesel and jet fuel balances in the US and Europe,” he says.
In addition, Abu Dhabi National Oil Company's decision to align Murban crude pricing with Dubai Platts from 1 November is expected to enhance pricing transparency and improve procurement flexibility for Asian refiners.
“Overall, the combination of the Russian waiver, increased Middle Eastern supply, the UAE's evolving position within OPEC, and the Murban pricing changes is positive for Indian refiners, strengthening their potential to increase diesel and jet fuel exports and generate economic benefits,” he adds.
The caveat
One very important point that is worth noting is that this waiver is for a 60-day period. This is clearly indicative that any relief from sanctions for Russia, and tariffs for countries like India is at best temporary as of now.
A day after suspending sanctions and tariffs linked to Russian exports, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that he had not yet made a final decision on the issue. Friday's executive order did not specify the duration of the waiver.
What Marco Rubio said about the waiver
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said the administration wanted additional time to assess the implications of the move.
Rubio said Trump would take up to 60 days to examine the economic consequences of the Russia-related sanctions and tariffs he had waived a day earlier.
Rubio said Trump had chosen to review the measures over a 60-day period.
"I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio said.
Separately, Rubio also appeared to recognise the practical considerations behind India's continued purchases of Russian crude.
The issue has been a key subject of discussions between him and External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar since the US passed the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act in September.
"You also can't unravel the economy of other countries because of one central issue. So that's the complex part of having to balance all of this,” Rubio said according to PTI.
Jaishankar is understood to have explained to Rubio that Indian refineries are largely designed to process medium-sour crude, which India sources from Middle Eastern countries and Russia.
He is also understood to have pointed out the differences in the grades of oil available from other suppliers. Venezuelan crude is heavier, while US oil is lighter and would need to be blended before Indian refineries could process it.
Will crude oil become cheaper for India?
For India, however, relief from tariffs does not necessarily mean cheaper oil. In fact, even globally despite America’s diesel supply deal with Russia and the sanctions waiver, crude oil prices continue to stay near $110 per barrel.
Pankaj Srivastava says the waiver was largely anticipated and is expected to provide modest support to crude prices while easing supply-side geopolitical risks for India.
As Natalia Katona points out: Removing the threat also removes a potential deterrent for competing buyers of Russian crude.
“So far, purchasing patterns show little sign of changing. For instance, China had already secured November-loading ESPO cargoes by early September, ahead of its usual buying schedule. India’s purchases by mid-October point to Russian crude flows of more or less the same 1.8 million b/d unchanged from September,” she tells TOI.
Brent Crude Price Trends
And, the pricing story is more complicated than the headline premium suggests.
According to Katona, the Urals deliveries to India are generally priced against Dated Brent, which reflects the tight physical crude market.
“Dated Brent was trading $20/bbl above ICE Brent futures for most of October and still is $10/bbl higher, therefore a cargo priced at Dated parity can still carry a substantial premium when compared to any other futures benchmark,” she explains.
Urals has moved from a premium of around $8/bbl to Dated Brent a month ago to roughly Dated parity today, with a possibility for that differential to soften further.
“Russian suppliers are adjusting to a higher physical benchmark and elevated freight costs to keep their barrels competitive. But a falling premium is not the same as a falling oil price,” she notes.
“India may negotiate a better differential with Russian grades and will still face a higher outright bill if the benchmark itself (in this case, Dated Brent) rises. With China competing for Russian barrels and global physical supplies tightening, the waiver eases India’s tariff risk without resolving its supply problem,” she adds.
But the weather may work in India’s favour over the coming months.
In September-October, a total of 12 cargoes carrying Russian oil transited the Northern Sea Route, on their way to China.
According to Katona, these flows should gradually halt as ice takes over most of the Arctic Ocean again, lowering the availability of Urals cargoes for China through the NSR.
“Considering India is generally closer to Russia geographically (entailing a lower freight cost), from November onwards Russian sellers of grades loading in European ports (Urals, Siberian Light or Russian CPC) should have a general prevalence for Indian deliveries,” she believes.

articles.title: Kyrgyzstan Exports Recover After Sharp Fall in Gold Sales - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: Kyrgyzstan Exports Recover After Sharp Fall in Gold Sales  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
Kyrgyzstan’s exports have begun to recover after a sharp decline in 2025, when the value of its gold exports plunged by nearly three-quarters. In the first eight months of 2026, exports rose by nearly 20%. Even so, for every dollar earned from selling goods overseas, Kyrgyzstan spent more than four dollars on imports.
According to a report by the National Statistical Committee of the Kyrgyz Republic, exports fell by 41.2% in 2025 to $3 billion. Imports, meanwhile, continued to grow, reaching $13.7 billion. As a result, the country spent $10.6 billion more on foreign goods than it earned from selling its own products abroad. A year earlier, the gap stood at $7.3 billion.
The main reason for the decline was a sharp drop in overseas sales of gold, one of Kyrgyzstan’s principal sources of export revenue. Their value fell from approximately $2.5 billion in 2024 to $683 million in 2025. Exports of other goods also fell 11.2%.
Trade was also affected by weaker demand from Russia and Kazakhstan, two major markets for Kyrgyz producers, as well as temporary restrictions on exports of certain goods, including scrap metal and livestock.
Kyrgyzstan’s trade is closely tied to neighboring countries. It belongs to the Eurasian Economic Union, alongside Russia, Kazakhstan, Belarus, and Armenia. Members trade with one another without standard customs duties on most goods. Russia and Kazakhstan remain the largest buyers of Kyrgyz products and, together with China, supply most imports.
The imbalance is particularly pronounced in trade with China. Chinese goods account for more than a third of Kyrgyzstan’s total imports, while China receives only around 5% of its exports. Uzbekistan also remains an important market for Kyrgyz products. Outside the region, Switzerland and the United Kingdom are significant destinations.
The downturn continued in the first half of 2026, when exports fell another 11.1% compared with the same period a year earlier.
By the end of August, however, the picture had changed. Figures for the first eight months showed exports rising 19.5% to $2.3 billion. Gold exports also rebounded sharply, reaching $770.6 million, more than in the whole of 2025. Over half of that amount was exported in August alone. Imports also increased, reaching $9.7 billion. The recovery in overseas sales has therefore not yet significantly narrowed the gap between exports and imports.
A trade deficit does not mean Kyrgyzstan is losing the equivalent amount from its government budget. It measures the difference between the value of goods imported into the country and those sold abroad. Imports are paid for by businesses and consumers, with funds coming from various sources, including remittances from migrant workers and investment.
Services have become one of the fastest-growing areas of Kyrgyzstan’s international trade, providing another source of funds for imports. According to preliminary figures, in 2025 the country earned $3.55 billion from services exports, up 20% from the previous year. Revenue from foreign visitors rose 36.9% to $1.19 billion. In international statistics, this category includes travelers’ spending on accommodation, food, shopping, and other services during their stay.
Revenue from financial services also increased, while earnings from transport and information technology services declined. Unlike its trade in goods, Kyrgyzstan exported more services than it imported, recording a services trade surplus of approximately $430 million in 2025.
Export growth in 2026 has interrupted a sharp downturn in overseas sales, but the overall picture remains largely unchanged. Kyrgyzstan continues to import large volumes of Chinese and Russian goods, while its exports remain heavily dependent on gold and demand from neighboring countries.
Kyrgyzstan’s government is developing measures to support exporters, including reducing transport costs and expanding businesses’ access to financing.

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. Uzbekistan has invited U.S. investors to participate in transport infrastructure and logistics projects, including the construction of New Tashkent International Airport, aircraft maintenance facilities, and cargo aircraft conversion centers.
According to the Uzbek Ministry of Transport, the investment opportunities were outlined by Transport Minister Ilkhom Makhkamov during a strategic panel session on energy and transport infrastructure at the Uzbekistan-U.S. business forum held on the sidelines of the C5+1 ministerial meeting in Samarkand on October 19.
Makhkamov highlighted the long-standing transport partnership between Uzbekistan and the United States, noting that Uzbekistan became the first Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) country to sign an Open Skies agreement with the United States in 1998. Direct flights currently operate between Tashkent and New York, while Uzbekistan Airways’ order for 22 Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft represents another milestone in bilateral cooperation, he said.
The minister identified transport and logistics as promising areas for U.S. investment, citing Uzbekistan’s strategic location at the crossroads of international transport corridors. He highlighted the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway project, along with plans to develop new road and rail infrastructure, as key initiatives to expand the country’s transit capacity.
Uzbekistan also plans to establish modern logistics centers in the Bukhara, Surkhandarya and Tashkent regions in 2027. The facilities are expected to expand cargo storage, processing and distribution services, strengthen international trade links and attract investment.
Makhkamov also highlighted opportunities to develop cold-storage facilities and rapid-delivery systems for Uzbekistan’s fruit and vegetable exports. articles.summary: From Samarkand to Washington: New Economic Opportunities in Uzbekistan–U.S. Cooperation  EIN News
articles.full_text:
Political trust, investment and advanced technologies mark a new stage in the strategic partnership.
TASHKENT, UZBEKISTAN, October 20, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- The Samarkand dialogue held on October 19, 2026, marked an important opportunity to strengthen Uzbekistan–U.S. relations and expand cooperation between the United States and Central Asia. The participation of Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio underscored the strategic importance of bilateral ties, with discussions focusing on trade, investment, industrial development, critical minerals, financial markets and advanced technologies.
The dialogue highlighted Uzbekistan’s growing role as a reliable international partner and a key link between Central Asia and global markets.
From Political Dialogue to Economic Results
A central priority in bilateral relations is translating political engagement into practical economic outcomes. The development of the Uzbekistan–U.S. Business and Investment Council is an important step towards strengthening direct contacts between governments, financial institutions and private-sector representatives, facilitating investment and addressing business challenges.
A total of 54 agreements and initiatives worth nearly $12 billion have been reported in connection with bilateral engagement. These initiatives reflect growing commercial interest and the potential to develop long-term partnerships.
For Uzbekistan, cooperation with the United States offers opportunities to attract capital, introduce advanced technologies and develop higher-value industries. American businesses, in turn, can access Uzbekistan’s expanding market and explore opportunities across Central Asia.
Trade and Investment on the Rise
Bilateral trade has grown significantly, increasing from approximately $215 million in 2017 to nearly $1 billion in 2025—around 4.7 times higher.
The positive trend continued in 2026. During the first eight months, bilateral trade reached $810.4 million, a 33.4 per cent increase compared with the same period in 2025. Uzbekistan’s exports to the United States amounted to $304.5 million, up 59.9 per cent, while imports from the United States totalled approximately $506 million, an increase of 21.3 per cent.
Further growth is possible in manufacturing, agriculture, energy, transport and information technology, where both countries can benefit from complementary capabilities.
Investment is another important pillar of the partnership. As of September 1, 2026, 377 companies with U.S. investment were operating in Uzbekistan. Between 2017 and 2025, the country attracted more than $2.9 billion in U.S. direct investment and loans.
These figures reflect expanding business engagement and the opportunities associated with Uzbekistan’s economic reforms, market development and efforts to improve the investment climate.
Financial Markets and Strategic Industries
The planned initial public offering of Uzbekistan’s National Investment Fund, valued at approximately $700 million, represents another step towards developing capital markets and attracting international investors.
The fund consolidates stakes in 13 state-owned enterprises, with international investment management company Franklin Templeton involved in its management. The initiative aims to strengthen corporate governance, improve transparency and promote more efficient asset management. Its success will depend on consistent implementation and sustained investor confidence.
Cooperation is also expanding into strategic industries, including critical minerals, advanced technologies, innovation and space-related activities.
Uzbekistan’s natural resources and geographical position create opportunities to develop mineral processing and supply chains for modern industries. For the United States, such cooperation can help diversify supply sources; for Uzbekistan, it offers the prospect of moving beyond raw-material exports towards higher-value production.
Technology partnerships can support industrial modernisation, digitalisation, skills development and the integration of Uzbek businesses into international value chains.
Uzbekistan’s accession to the Artemis Accords as the 77th signatory further demonstrates its interest in international cooperation on the peaceful exploration and use of outer space, creating potential opportunities for scientific exchange and technological development.
Strengthening Central Asia’s Global Position
The Uzbekistan–U.S. partnership also has a broader regional dimension. Improved connectivity, trade facilitation, infrastructure development and diversified economic partnerships are essential to Central Asia’s long-term prosperity.
Uzbekistan’s efforts to strengthen relations with neighbouring countries and expand international economic links can complement deeper engagement with the United States. Investment and commercial cooperation can support cross-border business activities, open new markets and strengthen the region’s integration into the global economy.
For international partners, a more connected and economically dynamic Central Asia offers opportunities for trade and investment. For regional countries, broader partnerships can diversify economic relations and support sustainable development.
The Samarkand dialogue therefore represents more than a diplomatic meeting: it provides a platform for advancing regional cooperation and strengthening Central Asia’s role in international economic relations.
Turning Commitments into Sustainable Results
The development of Uzbekistan–U.S. relations demonstrates a growing shift from political dialogue towards practical cooperation. Rising trade, expanding investment, new financial instruments and engagement in strategic industries provide a foundation for further progress.
The key indicators underline this potential: bilateral trade approached $1 billion in 2025; trade reached $810.4 million in the first eight months of 2026; 377 companies with U.S. investment operated in Uzbekistan as of September 1, 2026; and U.S. direct investment and loans attracted between 2017 and 2025 exceeded $2.9 billion. In addition, 54 agreements and initiatives valued at nearly $12 billion and the planned $700 million National Investment Fund IPO highlight the scale of economic ambitions.
Realising these opportunities will require transparent institutions, consistent reforms, effective implementation of agreements and stronger links between businesses.
By building on the momentum generated in Samarkand, Uzbekistan and the United States can deepen their strategic partnership, expand mutually beneficial economic cooperation and create new opportunities for investors, businesses and people across both countries and the wider Central Asian region.

articles.title: At the negotiating table and on the battlefield, Russia and Ukraine are at an impasse - CNN
articles.summary: At the negotiating table and on the battlefield, Russia and Ukraine are at an impasse  CNN
articles.full_text:
It’s like two theatrical performances unfolding side by side, before an audience of one.
The peace process surrounding Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has reached a remarkable impasse.
On one stage, European allies and Kyiv are scrambling to turn US demands and threats into something resembling a plan that might satisfy President Donald Trump. On the other, the Kremlin has its own show: envoy Kirill Dmitriev offers business opportunities designed to appeal to a mercantile US president, draw him further into Moscow’s orbit and allow Russia’s crawling frontline advance to proceed. Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, flit between the two productions. Yet the two plots remain separate and contemptuous of each other, with no denouement in sight.
When Trump speaks of a deal with Russia, one fact outweighs all others: Moscow’s idea of peace is basically victory. The Kremlin has been blunt about its demands, even in their least maximalist form. Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to surrender the Donbas without further fighting. He has also long entertained Ukraine’s demilitarization, a pledge never to join NATO and a change of leadership in Kyiv — all impractical or impossible in wartime. Russia’s pragmatist-in-chief has therefore settled on the Donbas as an attainable negotiating goal, while pressure grows on Kyiv to concede.
Why does Zelensky not simply yield? Reasons to do so grow as what remains of the Donbas becomes less habitable by the day. Russian drones stalk Kramatorsk, the largest population center, hunting civilians around the clock. Sloviansk, Dobropillia and Kostyantynivka are either ruins or targets for Russian glide bombs: places of great military importance, but little remaining civilian life.
            Yet the clearest case for why Ukraine cannot simply abandon the Donbas came from none other than Trump’s National security adviser, and possible successor, Marco Rubio. Russia controls all but 11% of the Donetsk region, while Ukraine describes the remainder as the “defensive line that they’ve embedded themselves in,” he said, in an interview with Breitbart News. “They argue, and military strategists say is true, that it is the last defensible line… From there, it’s just a straight shot into Kyiv.” He added that Russia is not really advancing and has therefore switched to “applying extraordinary pain on the people of Ukraine through drone strikes, through ballistic missile strikes, trying to destroy their energy infrastructure, their electricity.” Ukraine, in turn, is striking Russian refineries.
    
He acknowledged Kushner and Witkoff’s efforts, but ultimately concluded: “We’d like the war to end, but ultimately we also have other priorities around the world we’re focused on as well.”
Rubio spent 45 minutes on the phone with Zelensky on Tuesday, suggesting he may be more invested in the outcome than this closing remark implies. But his lowered expectations reflect the reality of these two separate onstage peace performances. Ukraine wants to survive; Russia wants to win, and still believes it can.
If one of the sounder minds in the White House sees peace as a long shot at best, what did the past 10 days of US-Ukrainian fallout achieve? Did it get Trump any closer to the deal he says he wants?
Trump has offered a striking array of pro-Russian incentives to draw Moscow towards a peace whose terms he has yet to define. It looks like pressure for its own sake — and to Putin’s immediate advantage.
            The list of Trump gifts to Moscow is extensive: a sudden diesel deal likely to throw billions into Putin’s war chest; an energy ceasefire (unilaterally announced by Trump and apparently unknown to either side), that slowed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for several days. There were also restrictions on vital Starlink technology that affected Ukraine’s defensive and offensive operations; limits on intelligence sharing that left Ukraine without warning of ballistic missile attacks for at least several nights; and repeated calls for Zelensky to leave office. Add to that the monthslong collapse of US financial support for Ukraine, with Europe now paying for military aid. If Putin could write US policy, it might look much like this.
    
Speaking in a news conference in Oslo after meeting with Witkoff in person and Kushner virtually, Zelensky said he hoped for a positive word from Rubio soon on the US-made Patriot air defense system and Starlink, while also saying that his country was “thankful that intelligence sharing” with the United States “now works.” Witkoff heads to Russia tomorrow and the nature of what he will present to Putin remains unclear.
Why now? The political damage Trump is inflicting on himself and his Republican colleagues ahead of the midterms is palpable. Some are struggling to distance themselves from this profoundly anti-American barrage of pro-Russian policies. Equally striking is how unsustainable or impractical many of these measures are. The diesel deal will not lower US pump prices quickly and European restrictions will probably limit how much cash it can deliver to Putin. The energy ceasefire was brief, absurd, and further undermined Trump’s credibility. Restrictions to Starlink, Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink controlled by the US government, and intelligence sharing appear to come and go, leaving Ukrainian troops in the lurch, while Rubio echoes Trump’s denial that any such limits ever existed.
This flurry of baffling activity makes sense only when seen through the US political prism. It is addressing the world after the midterm elections.
Zelensky has dispensed with the canard that pandering to Trump works. Ukraine is emotionally more adjusted to the idea of losing US support and going it alone, aware that survival is preferable to friendship with a fickle US. Europe knows there is a limited window now left in which Trump can do damage, and that whatever comes next is better. Even if it is more of the same, at least Europe and Ukraine will have had longer to prepare to go it alone.
Most troubling is Trump’s timing and thinking. He is only doing damage to his party and legacy. But with Republicans still in control of the House and Senate, and 2028’s race to succeed him not yet begun in earnest, perhaps he sees this as his last unbridled moment to express in practical ways his sympathy to someone apparently oddly important to him, as a US president: Vladimir Putin.

articles.title: Pope Leo urges Ukraine-Russia humanitarian cooperation as Russian strike kills children at playground - OSV News
articles.summary: Pope Leo urges Ukraine-Russia humanitarian cooperation as Russian strike kills children at playground  OSV News
articles.full_text:
(OSV News) — Pope Leo XIV spoke by phone with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, expressing hope that Ukraine and Russia will cooperate on humanitarian aid and evacuations for civilians in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky, the Vatican said.
In an Oct. 19 statement, the Vatican press office said the conversation centered on “the grave situation” in the city, which has been under Russian military occupation since 2022.
Pope Leo’s phone call with Zelenskyy came less than a week after an Oct. 13 call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, while the pontiff was recovering from lung surgery at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital. In that call, the pope requested a humanitarian ceasefire, the Vatican said.
“His Holiness expressed the hope that cooperation between both parties will allow for the delivery of food and medical aid, and for the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population,” the statement read.
The pope also reaffirmed the Holy See’s commitment “to promoting dialogue and peace.”
In a separate statement published Oct. 19 by the Ukrainian president’s office, Zelenskyy said he wished the pope “full and speedy recovery following surgery.”
“We are grateful that even during this difficult time for him personally, His Holiness remembers Ukraine and prays for our people,” Zelenskyy said.
According to his office, Zelenskyy gave the pope a detailed briefing on Russian strikes against Ukrainian cities, and the two “discussed the humanitarian catastrophe” in Oleshky.
Zelenskyy, the statement read, “noted that Ukraine is working to help our people there and is preparing the necessary decisions. His Holiness informed him about contacts with the Russian side on this matter.”
Tensions with Washington
Zelenskyy also briefed Pope Leo on reported disruptions to Ukraine’s defense communications, which have strained relations with Washington. According to NPR, Zelenskyy said SpaceX imposed restrictions on the country’s access to the U.S. military’s Starshield satellite internet network in response “to a message from the American government.”
Starshield is a military version of Starlink, the satellite internet service run by SpaceX, the aerospace company founded by Elon Musk.
Musk, however, denied that SpaceX played any role in the disruptions, saying that “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government” and that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately” by U.S. President Donald Trump.
Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also denied Zelenskyy’s claim that the US government ordered the disruptions, NPR reported.
Nevertheless, tensions between Ukraine and the United States have risen after Trump moved to waive sanctions against Russia in exchange for purchasing diesel in an attempt to lower rising prices due to war in Iran.
Zelenskyy’s office said the Ukrainian president’s conversation with Pope Leo “covered current security challenges and threats, including the periodic lack of warnings from partners about Russian ballistic missile attacks, which has happened three times recently.”
“The president thanked His Holiness for his support and all his efforts to achieve a dignified peace,” the statement read.
Decrying crimes against humanity
In a message marking the war’s 244th week, Major Archbishop Sviatoslav Shevchuk of Kyiv-Halych, head of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church, condemned Russia’s attacks against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
According to the Reuters news agency, Trump announced an energy ceasefire Oct. 11; however, neither Russia nor Ukraine confirmed the agreement.
Despite the so-called truce, Russia has continued to conduct attacks on Ukraine’s energy grid, which left 600,000 people without electricity, Major Archbishop Shevchuk wrote.
“Crimes against humanity of this kind were committed precisely when the U.S. president announced a so-called energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine,” Major Archbishop Shevchuk wrote, calling the timing of the attacks especially painful.
“It is … very important for us, as Christians, to understand that even peace negotiations and efforts to end a war must be governed by moral principles,” Major Archbishop Shevchuk added, saying that “Agreements reached without regard for such principles, in which energy resources are valued more highly than human life, are doomed to fail.”
On Oct. 19, Iranian-designed Russian Shahed drones killed six people and injured 14 in the Kharkiv region, an attack Zelenskyy called a “pure atrocity.” A one-year-old girl named Angelina was killed in the strike, with her mother Inna dying hours later in the hospital, Zelenskyy wrote in his post on X.
“These are horrific photos, but behind them are shattered lives and the truth about this war,” he said, sharing photographs from the playground where the attack occurred, killing among others an 11-year-old girl.
The head of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church said negotiations shouldn’t ignore the human cost and that any agreements must be assessed by “the extent to which they alleviate the suffering” of the people and not by “the political or economic benefits they yield or the high-profile political statements they generate.”
“And even as we gratefully acknowledge mediation efforts aimed at ending the war, it is essential to distinguish between restraining an unjust aggressor and coercing the victim,” Major Archbishop Shevchuk wrote.
He also reminded the international community that while Ukraine depends on aid, that dependence “gives no one the moral right to dictate its future without the participation of the Ukrainian people themselves.”
“We must not blur the distinction between the aggressor state and the people who have the right to defend themselves,” Major Archbishop Shevchuk wrote. “In international efforts to end any war — including Russia’s war against Ukraine — it is essential not to set peace against justice.”
– – – 
Junno Arocho Esteves is an international correspondent for OSV News. Follow him on X @jae_journalist.

articles.title: A diesel tank burns at Transneft’s Druzhba hub as Ukraine keeps striking Russian energy despite Trump’s pressure - Euromaidan Press
articles.summary: A diesel tank burns at Transneft’s Druzhba hub as Ukraine keeps striking Russian energy despite Trump’s pressure  Euromaidan Press
articles.full_text:
Drones attacked an oil and fuel pumping station of Russia’s Druzhba pipeline system in Tambov Oblast overnight on 20 October, setting a diesel tank on fire, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported, citing locals. Druzhba, Russian for “friendship,” is a Soviet-era oil pipeline, about 4,000 km long, that carries Russian crude west to Europe, including through a branch that crosses Ukraine. The struck station is on its Russian section. Tambov Oblast Governor Yevgeny Pervyshov confirmed a fire at an unnamed enterprise in Michurinsk district after what he called a Ukrainian drone attack. The station lies about 400 km from the front line.
Ukraine has spent months striking the refineries, terminals, and pipelines that fund Russia’s war, and its Defense Ministry says the strikes have knocked out more than half of Russia’s refining capacity. Washington wants them stopped. US officials reportedly tied intelligence sharing to a halt in refinery strikes, and US President Donald Trump called their resumption “a disgrace.”
Hours of attack before dawn
Russia’s regional alert system declared a drone threat at 03:38, Ukrainian military outlet Militarnyi reported. By 06:25, Exilenova+ said the Nikolskoye station was under attack, after Michurinsk had been under attack for several hours.
Pervyshov said four Ukrainian drones were shot down over the region and no one was hurt. He did not name the site.
Ukraine has not commented. The General Staff’s 20 October list of overnight strikes does not mention Tambov Oblast.
A Druzhba fuel hub hit before
The Nikolskoye station belongs to Transneft, Russia’s state pipeline operator. It stores and pumps crude oil and refined fuels, including diesel, gasoline, and jet fuel. The complex has three tank farms and two pumping stations, and it can move up to 300,000 tonnes a day, according to Current Time.
Ukrainian drones hit a station of the same hub in August 2025, and Ukraine’s General Staff said then that pumping on the pipeline had stopped completely.
Strikes resume despite US pressure
Ukraine paused refinery strikes for three days after Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” on 11 October, while Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s grid. Since Kyiv resumed the strikes, drones have also hit an oil terminal and a fuel depot in St. Petersburg.
Kyiv reads other US moves as pressure too, from missed warnings of Russian ballistic launches to a Starlink cap that slows Ukrainian drones. President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy told US senators he had offered a 30-day halt on refinery strikes in exchange for Patriot interceptors, but Trump’s envoys showed no openness.
